'''Elayne Arrington''' (born {{circa|1940}}) is an American [[mathematician]] and [[engineer]]. She was the first [[African Americans|African American]] woman to graduate with a bachelor's degree from the School of Engineering at the [[University of Pittsburgh]]. After earning her Ph.D., she went on to conduct performance analyses of [[Soviet Union]] aircraft at the [[Wright-Patterson Air Force Base]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.bizjournals.com/pittsburgh/news/2017/02/15/pioneer-role-model-for-next-generation.html|title=Pioneer role model for next generation|last=Wojcik|first=Joe|date=15 February 2017|website=www.bizjournals.com|access-date=2018-05-30}}</ref><ref name=":2">{{Cite web|last=Rouvalis|first=Cristina|title=Against the Odds|url=https://www.pittmag.pitt.edu/news/against-odds|access-date=2020-11-06|website=Pitt Magazine|language=en}}</ref>

== Early life and education ==
Elayne Arrington grew up in [[West Mifflin, Pennsylvania]]. She graduated from Homestead High School (now [[Steel Valley School District|Steel Valley High School]]) in 1957 where she received the second-highest [[SAT]] score in mathematics (797 out of 800).<ref name=":1">{{Cite web|url=https://www.pts.edu/Elayne_Arrington|title=Elayne Arrington|website=www.pts.edu|language=en|access-date=2018-05-30}}</ref> Despite finishing first in her class, Elayne was denied the opportunity to deliver the valedictory address. Instead school administrators assigned the speech to the class president who was white and male.<ref name=":1" />

Arrington was recommended for a full-ride scholarship to study [[mechanical engineering]] at the University of Pittsburgh. Still, the sponsor, the Mesta Machine Company, withdrew her scholarship, saying that the money had to be given to a man because women "do not finish engineering programs."<ref name=":4">{{Cite news|url=https://www.post-gazette.com/opinion/Op-Ed/2017/02/09/Robert-Hill-Pittsburgh-s-own-Hidden-Figures/stories/201702280022|title=Robert Hill: Pittsburgh's own 'Hidden Figures'|work=Pittsburgh Post-Gazette|access-date=2018-05-30|language=en}}</ref> In spite of that prediction, in 1961 Arrington became the first African-American woman to graduate from the University of Pittsburgh's School of Engineering. As a member of the engineering honorary [[Pi Tau Sigma]].<ref name=":4" /> She discussed the nature of the obstacles she faced to Rouvalis.<ref name=":2" /> {{blockquote|"Some of [the barriers] may have been racial prejudice, but they didn't even have to get to racial because being a girl in engineering, being female, was enough."<ref name=":2" /> }}Arrington went on to earn a [[Master's degree|master's]] degree in mathematics from the [[University of Dayton]] in Ohio, and while working on her master's Arrington, a Charles Phelps Taft Fellow, also took math courses at [[University of Oxford|Oxford University]].<ref name=":2" /><ref name=":1" /> She earned her Ph.D. in math at the [[University of Cincinnati]] in 1974 with a thesis titled ''The P-Frattini Subgroup of a Finite Group,'' supervised by Donald B. Parker.<ref name=":2" /><ref>{{Cite web|last=|first=|date=|title=University of Cincinnati Mathematics PhD Alumni|url=https://www.artsci.uc.edu/departments/math/grad/phd-grads.html|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200610160050/https://www.artsci.uc.edu/departments/math/grad/phd-grads.html |archive-date=2020-06-10 |access-date=|website=}}</ref> She became the 17th African-American woman in the United States to earn a [[Doctor of Philosophy|PhD]] in mathematics.<ref name=":1" /><ref name=":0">{{Cite news|url=http://swsg.org/four-inspiring-african-american-women-honored-at-university-of-pittsburgh/|title=Four Inspiring African-American Women Honored at University of Pittsburgh - SWSG|date=2017-07-20|work=SWSG|access-date=2018-05-30|language=en-US}}</ref>

== Career ==
Arrington was hired as an [[Aerospace engineering|aerospace engineer]] in the Foreign Technology Division at [[Wright-Patterson Air Force Base]] in [[Dayton, Ohio]].<ref name=":0" /> At the base, she analyzed the performance of [[Soviet Union]] aircraft.<ref name=":0" />

In 1974 with her newly earned doctorate, she returned to the University of Pittsburgh where she taught in the department of mathematics and statistics. Arrington cut back her work schedule in 2012, and fully retired from the university in 2018.<ref name=":2" /><ref name=":1" /><ref name=":3">{{Cite web|title=6 Apr 2007, Page 12 - Pittsburgh Post-Gazette at Newspapers.com|url=http://www.newspapers.com/image/96645609/?terms=Elayne%20Arrington&match=1|access-date=2020-11-10|website=Newspapers.com|language=en}}</ref>

In 2007, she was named a [[Community College of Allegheny County]] board member.<ref name=":3" />

In 2016, Arrington took a class at the [[Pittsburgh Theological Seminary]] in [[New Testament]] [[Greek language|Greek]] "so she could read the [[Bible]] in its original language."<ref name=":2" /> She pursued theological studies classes at the University of Pittsburgh and plans to complete her studies in 2021 at the age of 81, for another master's degree, this one in theological study.<ref name=":2" />

== Awards ==
In April 2007, Arrington received a Distinguished Alumnus Award from the University of Pittsburgh's African American Alumni Council.<ref name=":0" />
